n151364091: Town and Country: the name is the whole plan. Back in eighteen eighty-six this was farm country called Altheim. In nineteen fifty a tiny village of just one hundred sixty-two people decided to stay a mix of town and country, homes tucked between woods and fields, and today it's one of the wealthiest cities in Missouri. But the loudest day in its history was about golf. The famous Bellerive Country Club is here; it hosted the U.S. Open in nineteen sixty-five and the PGA Championship twice. In August twenty eighteen, at the hundredth PGA Championship, Brooks Koepka won with a record score while Tiger Woods charged with a sixty-four on the final day, his best ever last round in a major. The roars rolled across these hills. And here's something close to home for us: just past the city line, across from Queeny Park, is the Hindu Temple of St. Louis, serving thousands of families, with a shrine to Lord Venkateswara. The Telugu Association of St. Louis and the Tamil Sangam, which runs a Tamil school and a Pongal festival, bring together families from all around these suburbs. Mansions, golf and Balaji: quite a neighborhood!
n151890128: Ready for a love story? Creve Coeur is French for broken heart. The legend says a Native American princess fell for a French fur trapper who didn't love her back, and she leapt from a ledge above the lake, and the lake took the shape of a broken heart. Nobody knows if it's true, but the name stuck. For a long time this was just a string of little communities along Olive Street Road. After World War Two, as St. Louis pushed west, Creve Coeur became a city in December nineteen forty-nine. The big news came from business: Monsanto, the giant seed and farm-science company, had its headquarters here until Bayer bought it in twenty eighteen, and Drury Hotels is still based here. Just north is Creve Coeur Lake, the county's oldest park. Back around nineteen hundred, a streetcar line brought city families out to an amusement park called Electric Park, and today rowers glide across the water. And here's something close to home for us: along Olive Boulevard, a restaurant called Tabla serves dosa, idiyappam and thatte idli. A broken heart, mended with a good dosa!
n5336773606: Here's a name with a secret older than St. Louis itself. Des Peres means of the fathers in French. Around December seventeen hundred, a band of Kaskaskia people and French settlers, with Jesuit priests, the fathers, set up a little mission by a river near the Mississippi. It's believed to be one of the very first European settlements in all of Missouri. The mission lasted only about three years, but the river kept the name, River des Peres, and the name kept traveling. When this area became a town in nineteen thirty-four, nobody even suggested another name; everyone already called it Des Peres. Fast forward to nineteen sixty-nine: West County Center opened here, a mall that became the big weekend outing for West County families. It closed in two thousand one and was rebuilt as a brand-new mall the very next year. And here's something close to home for us: just a short drive west is the Hindu Temple of St. Louis, where Diwali ends with fireworks lighting up the temple grounds, and on Manchester Road you can find Indian kitchens like Flavors. Priests, prayers and fireworks: Des Peres has always been about the fathers, and the families!
n569768151: Here comes Chesterfield, and it's a comeback story. Not long ago this was quiet farmland in west St. Louis County, and it only became a city in nineteen eighty-eight. Five years later came the night nobody here forgets. July thirtieth, nineteen ninety-three, the Great Flood: the Missouri River smashed through the Monarch Levee, and the whole valley, once nicknamed Gumbo Flats, filled with more than eight feet of muddy water. People came back, built higher levees, and the valley grew bigger than ever, with one of the largest strip malls in America. Now the fun part: Faust Park, with the Butterfly House, where thousands of butterflies float around you, and the old St. Louis Carousel. Right there stands Thornhill, built in eighteen nineteen, the oldest governor's home still standing in Missouri. It belonged to Frederick Bates, the state's second governor, whose brother Edward became Abraham Lincoln's Attorney General. And here's something close to home for us: Indian families have been moving to Chesterfield for jobs, and just down the road is the Hindu Temple of St. Louis, which has a shrine to Lord Venkateswara, our Balaji. So yes, you can get darshan near a butterfly house!
n6281417974: Okay, everyone, look out the window, because Weldon Spring has a secret. Picture the seventeen-nineties: a frontiersman named John Weldon builds a log home beside a bubbling spring here, on land Spain still owned. A quiet farm country grows up around it. Then, in World War Two, the Army arrives, moves out three whole little towns, Howell, Hamburg and Toonerville, and builds what was called the largest explosives factory in America, cranking out TNT. In nineteen fifty-five a uranium plant follows. When the country finally cleaned it all up, a story that made national news, they sealed the waste inside a giant stone-covered hill, seventy-five feet tall, finished in two thousand one. And here's the twist: today families climb the stairs to the top just for the view, and the old factory land has turned into the Busch and Weldon Spring conservation areas, with deer, lakes and the Katy Trail along the Missouri River. And something close to home: here in St. Charles County, one Indian family has opened their backyard every Diwali for more than ten years, lighting lamps with their neighbors. From TNT to diyas, not bad for one little spring!
